22-sharks-trees.name: Sharks Older Than Trees
22-sharks-trees.idea: Sharks appeared about 450 million years ago, tens of millions of years before the first trees, and survived all five mass extinctions.
22-sharks-trees.title: Sharks are OLDER than trees
22-sharks-trees.body: The first shark-like fish swam about 450 million years ago. The first true trees only appeared around 385 million years ago. Sharks have since survived all five mass extinctions.

23-moon-face.name: Moon Same Face
23-moon-face.idea: The Moon spins once per orbit (tidal locking), so the same side always faces Earth.
23-moon-face.title: Why we only EVER see one side of the Moon
23-moon-face.hook: The Moon does spin. Here's the catch.
23-moon-face.body: The Moon spins exactly once for every trip around Earth. Long ago Earth's gravity tugged on the Moon's slight bulge until its spin matched its orbit. That's tidal locking.

24-cat-feet.name: Cats Land On Feet
24-cat-feet.idea: Cats use the righting reflex: inner ear, a front-then-back twist, a flexible spine and a floating collarbone.
24-cat-feet.title: How cats ALWAYS land on their feet
24-cat-feet.hook: Drop a cat and watch it flip.
24-cat-feet.body: It's the righting reflex. The inner ear finds 'up', the cat twists its front half then its back half, using a bendy spine and a floating collarbone, then spreads out like a parachute.

25-popcorn.name: Why Popcorn Pops
25-popcorn.idea: Water sealed inside each kernel turns to steam; pressure bursts the hull and the starch puffs into foam.
25-popcorn.title: Why popcorn POPS
25-popcorn.hook: Every kernel is a tiny pressure cooker.
25-popcorn.body: Each kernel holds a drop of water sealed in by a tough shell. Heat turns it to steam until the pressure is about ten times normal air pressure, the shell bursts, and the starch puffs out and sets.

26-liberty-green.name: Statue of Liberty Green
26-liberty-green.idea: The copper Statue of Liberty was reddish-brown in 1886 and turned green over about 30 years as a protective patina formed.
26-liberty-green.title: The Statue of Liberty USED to be brown
26-liberty-green.body: When it was finished in 1886 the statue was shiny reddish-brown copper, like a new penny. Over about 30 years air and rain built up a green patina, which now protects the metal, so it is never cleaned off.

27-big-ben.name: Big Ben Is A Bell
27-big-ben.idea: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell; the tower was the Clock Tower, renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
27-big-ben.title: Big Ben is NOT the tower
27-big-ben.hook: Everyone gets this wrong about London.
27-big-ben.body: Big Ben is the nickname of the 13.7-tonne great bell, ringing since 1859. The tower was simply the Clock Tower until 2012, when it became the Elizabeth Tower for the Queen's Diamond Jubilee.

28-bubbles-round.name: Why Bubbles Are Round
28-bubbles-round.idea: Surface tension shrinks a soap film to the least area for the air inside, and that shape is a sphere.
28-bubbles-round.title: Why bubbles are ALWAYS round
28-bubbles-round.hook: Even a square wand makes a round bubble.
28-bubbles-round.body: Soap film acts like a stretchy skin that always tries to shrink. For any amount of air, the shape with the least surface is a sphere, so the film pulls itself into a ball.

29-everest-mauna-kea.name: Everest Not Tallest
29-everest-mauna-kea.idea: Everest is highest above sea level, but Mauna Kea is over 10,000 m tall from its base on the ocean floor.
29-everest-mauna-kea.title: Everest is NOT the tallest mountain
29-everest-mauna-kea.hook: Highest isn't the same as tallest.
29-everest-mauna-kea.body: Everest's peak is about 8,849 m above sea level. Mauna Kea in Hawaii pokes only about 4,207 m above the sea, but measured from its base on the ocean floor it is over 10,000 m tall.

30-stars-twinkle.name: Why Stars Twinkle
30-stars-twinkle.idea: Stars are point sources, so air turbulence bends their thin beam; planets are tiny discs whose wobbles average out.
30-stars-twinkle.title: Why stars twinkle but planets DON'T
30-stars-twinkle.body: Starlight arrives as a single point, so moving air bends it around and it flickers. Planets are closer and show a tiny disc, so the wobbles average out and they shine steady. From space, stars don't twinkle at all.

31-goosebumps.name: Why Goosebumps
31-goosebumps.idea: A tiny muscle under each hair pulls it upright; for furry ancestors this trapped warm air or made them look bigger.
31-goosebumps.title: Why we get GOOSEBUMPS
31-goosebumps.hook: Goosebumps are left over from our furry past.
31-goosebumps.body: A tiny muscle under every hair pulls it upright when you're cold or scared. For furry ancestors that fluffed the fur to trap warm air or look bigger. We lost the fur but kept the reflex.
